Key characteristics: created automatically by Kubernetes, reserved for system components, contains critical Pods and Services that keep the cluster running. Components that typically run in kube-system: API Server, Controller Manager, Scheduler, etcd (may run in kube-system or have their own namespace), CoreDNS (or kube-dns), kube-proxy, Metrics Server, Node Exporter, various admission controllers. Important: Do not create or modify objects in kube-system unless you are a cluster administrator. Deleting or modifying objects in kube-system can cause cluster instability or failure. You can view system components using kubectl get pods -n kube-system.

questions.question: What is kube-public Namespace?
options: Namespace for public resources, readable by all users
questions.correctAnswer: Namespace for public resources, readable by all users
questions.explanation: The kube-public Namespace is for public resources that should be readable by all users, even unauthenticated users.
questions.detailedAnswer: The kube-public Namespace is a special Namespace that contains information that should be publicly readable (i.e., accessible without authentication). It is automatically created by Kubernetes and is world-readable. Key characteristics: exists by default in all Kubernetes clusters, accessible to all users (even unauthenticated users in some configurations), contains ConfigMaps that are meant to be publicly accessible. Common use case: Contains a ConfigMap with the cluster-info that includes the cluster API Server address and CA certificate. This allows unauthenticated users to discover the API Server endpoint. Important: Be cautious about what you put in kube-public, as it is accessible to all users. Only put information here that is truly public and not sensitive. Most objects should not be placed in kube-public.

questions.question: What is a Context in kubectl?
options: Combination of cluster, Namespace, and user
questions.correctAnswer: Combination of cluster, Namespace, and user
questions.explanation: A Context in kubectl is a combination of a cluster, a Namespace, and a user, allowing quick switching between different configurations.
questions.detailedAnswer: A Context in kubectl is a combination of a cluster, a user, and a Namespace. It allows you to quickly switch between different configurations without having to specify all the details each time. Contexts are stored in the kubectl configuration file (typically ~/.kube/config). Key components: cluster (API Server URL and CA certificate), user (credentials for authentication), namespace (default Namespace for commands). Commands: kubectl config get-contexts (list all contexts), kubectl config current-context (show current context), kubectl config use-context <name> (switch to a context), kubectl config set-context <name> --namespace=<ns> (set default namespace for a context), kubectl config delete-context <name> (delete a context). Contexts are useful for managing multiple clusters (e.g., dev, staging, production) or multiple users.

questions.question: What is RBAC in Kubernetes?
questions.correctAnswer: Role-Based Access Control for authorization
questions.explanation: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) is an authorization mechanism that uses Roles and RoleBindings to control access to Kubernetes resources.
questions.detailedAnswer: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) is a method of regulating access to Kubernetes resources based on roles and permissions. It allows you to define fine-grained access policies for users, groups, and service accounts. RBAC is enabled by default in Kubernetes v1.8 and later. Key concepts: Role (set of permissions within a Namespace), ClusterRole (set of permissions across the entire cluster), RoleBinding (assigns a Role to a user/group within a Namespace), ClusterRoleBinding (assigns a ClusterRole to a user/group across the entire cluster), Subject (user, group, or service account that receives permissions). RBAC is rule-based - you define what actions (verbs) can be performed on which resources (resource types) in which namespaces.

questions.question: What is a Role in RBAC?
options: Set of permissions within a Namespace
Set of permissions across all Namespaces
questions.correctAnswer: Set of permissions within a Namespace
questions.explanation: A Role in RBAC defines a set of permissions (rules) within a single Namespace, specifying what operations are allowed on which resources.
questions.detailedAnswer: A Role in RBAC is a Kubernetes object that defines a set of permissions within a specific Namespace. It lists which operations (verbs) can be performed on which resources (resource types). Key components: rules (array of Rule objects), each Rule has: apiGroups (list of API groups), resources (list of resource types), verbs (list of allowed actions). Example: A Role that allows read access to Pods in a Namespace. Roles are Namespace-scoped - they only apply to resources within their Namespace. Roles are used in conjunction with RoleBindings to grant permissions to specific users or groups. Common verbs: get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete, exec.

questions.question: What is a ClusterRole in RBAC?
options: Set of permissions across all Namespaces
Set of permissions within a Namespace
questions.correctAnswer: Set of permissions across all Namespaces
questions.explanation: A ClusterRole in RBAC defines a set of permissions across all Namespaces in the cluster, specifying what operations are allowed on which resources.
questions.detailedAnswer: A ClusterRole in RBAC is similar to a Role, but it applies across the entire cluster rather than being limited to a single Namespace. It defines a set of permissions that can be applied to all Namespaces or to specific Namespaces through ClusterRoleBindings. Key components: same as Role (rules with apiGroups, resources, verbs). ClusterRoles are used for: cluster-wide permissions (e.g., Node access, PersistentVolume access), non-Namespace-scoped resources (e.g., Nodes, PersistentVolumes), permissions that need to be applied to multiple Namespaces. ClusterRoles are used in conjunction with ClusterRoleBindings to grant permissions to specific users or groups. ClusterRoles can also be used with RoleBindings to grant permissions within specific Namespaces.

questions.question: What is a RoleBinding in RBAC?
options: Grants Role permissions to users within a Namespace
questions.correctAnswer: Grants Role permissions to users within a Namespace
questions.explanation: A RoleBinding grants the permissions defined in a Role to a user or group of users within a specific Namespace.
questions.detailedAnswer: A RoleBinding in RBAC is a Kubernetes object that assigns a Role to a specific user, group, or service account within a specific Namespace. It connects the Role (which defines permissions) to the Subject (which receives the permissions). Key components: subjects (array of Subject objects, each with kind, name, and optionally namespace or apiGroup), roleRef (reference to the Role being assigned). The binding only applies to the Namespace where the RoleBinding is created. RoleBindings grant the permissions defined in the Role to the specified Subjects within the specified Namespace. Multiple RoleBindings can reference the same Role, and multiple Subjects can be assigned to the same Role through a single RoleBinding.

questions.question: What is a ClusterRoleBinding in RBAC?
options: Grants ClusterRole permissions across all Namespaces
questions.correctAnswer: Grants ClusterRole permissions across all Namespaces
questions.explanation: A ClusterRoleBinding grants the permissions defined in a ClusterRole to a user or group of users across all Namespaces in the cluster.
questions.detailedAnswer: A ClusterRoleBinding in RBAC is similar to a RoleBinding, but it assigns a ClusterRole to users, groups, or service accounts across the entire cluster. It connects the ClusterRole (which defines permissions) to the Subject (which receives the permissions). Key components: same as RoleBinding (subjects, roleRef). ClusterRoleBindings grant the permissions defined in the ClusterRole to the specified Subjects across all Namespaces. They can also be used to grant access to cluster-scoped resources (e.g., Nodes, PersistentVolumes). Use ClusterRoleBinding when you need to grant cluster-wide permissions. Use RoleBinding when you need to grant permissions within a specific Namespace.

questions.question: What is a ServiceAccount?
options: Provides identity for processes in Pods
questions.correctAnswer: Provides identity for processes in Pods
questions.explanation: A ServiceAccount provides an identity for processes that run in Pods, allowing them to authenticate with the API Server and access resources based on RBAC permissions.
questions.detailedAnswer: A ServiceAccount provides an identity for processes that run in a Pod. It allows Pods to authenticate with the Kubernetes API Server and be authorized to perform specific actions based on RBAC rules. Key characteristics: every Pod has a ServiceAccount (defaults to default if not specified), ServiceAccounts are associated with specific Namespaces, each ServiceAccount has a set of credentials (tokens, CA certificates) stored as Secrets. Use cases: 1) Running applications that need to interact with the Kubernetes API, 2) Providing fine-grained permissions to Pods based on their ServiceAccount, 3) Enabling workload identity (e.g., in cloud environments). Each ServiceAccount has: a name, a Namespace, an associated Secret (containing the token), and associated RBAC roles. Commands: kubectl get serviceaccounts, kubectl create serviceaccount <name>, kubectl describe serviceaccount <name>. ServiceAccounts are critical for workload identity and security.

questions.question: What is default ServiceAccount?
options: ServiceAccount created automatically in each Namespace
questions.correctAnswer: ServiceAccount created automatically in each Namespace
questions.explanation: The default ServiceAccount is created automatically in each Namespace and is used by Pods that don't specify a ServiceAccount.
questions.detailedAnswer: The default ServiceAccount is automatically created in every Namespace and is used by Pods that do not explicitly specify a ServiceAccount. Every Pod has a ServiceAccount, and if you do not specify one in the Pod specification, the default ServiceAccount for that Namespace is used. Key characteristics: created automatically when a Namespace is created, has no special permissions by default, associated with a Secret that contains a token for API authentication. The default ServiceAccount is typically named default and can be viewed using kubectl get serviceaccount -n <namespace>. It is good practice to create custom ServiceAccounts for your Pods with specific RBAC roles rather than using the default ServiceAccount for everything. This enables better security and access control.

questions.question: What is kubectl config?
questions.correctAnswer: Manages kubectl configuration
questions.explanation: kubectl config is a command group for managing kubectl configuration, including contexts, clusters, and users.
questions.detailedAnswer: kubectl config is a set of commands for managing the kubectl configuration file. The configuration file (typically ~/.kube/config) stores information about clusters, users, contexts, and preferences. kubectl config commands allow you to: view and manage contexts (kubectl config get-contexts, kubectl config use-context), view and set the current context (kubectl config current-context), view and manage clusters (kubectl config get-clusters, kubectl config set-cluster), view and manage users (kubectl config get-users, kubectl config set-credentials), view and manage preferences (kubectl config set). The configuration file uses a hierarchical structure to store information about multiple clusters and users, making it easy to switch between different environments.

questions.question: What is kubectl get?
questions.correctAnswer: All of the above
questions.explanation: kubectl get is a versatile command that lists resources, retrieves resource details, and can display information in various formats.
questions.detailedAnswer: kubectl get is one of the most commonly used kubectl commands for listing and viewing Kubernetes resources. It retrieves information about resources from the API Server and displays it in a readable format. Syntax: kubectl get <resource-type> [options]. Common resource types: pods, services, deployments, replica sets, nodes, namespaces, configmaps, secrets, persistentvolumes, persistentvolumeclaims, jobs, cronjobs, ingresses. Common options: -n or --namespace (specify namespace), -o or --output (specify output format: wide, json, yaml), -l or --selector (filter by label), --all-namespaces or -A (list from all namespaces), --show-labels (show labels). Examples: kubectl get pods, kubectl get pods -n kube-system, kubectl get pods -o wide, kubectl get all, kubectl get pods --all-namespaces.

questions.question: What is kubectl describe?
options: Shows detailed information about a resource
questions.correctAnswer: Shows detailed information about a resource
questions.explanation: kubectl describe provides detailed information about a specific resource, including its configuration, status, and events.
questions.detailedAnswer: kubectl describe is a command that provides detailed information about a specific Kubernetes resource. It retrieves all the metadata and configuration details for the resource and displays it in a human-readable format. Syntax: kubectl describe <resource-type> <resource-name> [options]. Common resource types: pods, services, deployments, nodes, namespaces, etc. Common options: -n or --namespace (specify namespace). The describe command shows: metadata (name, namespace, labels, annotations), specification (full configuration), status (current state, conditions, events), events (recent events related to the resource, helpful for debugging). Examples: kubectl describe pod <pod-name>, kubectl describe node <node-name>, kubectl describe deployment <deployment-name>. This command is particularly useful for debugging and troubleshooting.

questions.question: What is kubectl logs?
questions.correctAnswer: Prints logs from Pod containers
questions.explanation: kubectl logs prints the logs from the containers in a Pod, useful for debugging and monitoring.
questions.detailedAnswer: kubectl logs is a command that retrieves and displays the logs from containers in a Pod. This is essential for debugging and monitoring running applications. Syntax: kubectl logs <pod-name> [options]. Common options: -c or --container (specify container name if Pod has multiple containers), --previous (show logs from previous instance of the container, useful for debugging crash loops), -f or --follow (stream logs in real-time), --since (show logs from a specific time), --tail (show last N lines). Examples: kubectl logs <pod-name> (show logs from the only container), kubectl logs <pod-name> -c <container-name> (show logs from specific container), kubectl logs -f <pod-name> (follow logs in real-time). For debugging crash loops: kubectl logs --previous <pod-name>.
